term: Page Analysis and Ground Truth Elements
definition: Page Analysis and Ground Truth Elements (PAGE) is an XML standard for encoding digitised documents.
details: Comparable to Analyzed Layout and Text Object (ALTO), it allows the organisation and structure of a page and its contents to be described. PAGE XML can be used to describe: page content (regions, lines of text, words, glyphs, reading order, text content, ...) the evaluation of the layout analysis (evaluation profiles, evaluation results, ...) the cutting of the document image (cutting grids) The format is developed by the Pattern Recognition & Image Analysis Lab (PRIMA) at the University of Salford in Manchester. It was designed to be used in conjunction with automatic segmentation and transcription techniques (optical character recognition (OCR) and handwritten text recognition (HTR)): indeed, PAGE aims to support each of the different steps in the processing chain for image document analysis (from image enhancement to layout analysis to OCR). The PAGE XML schema is used as an export and import format by automatic transcription software such as eScriptorium and Transkribus. It is also an export format used by Kraken, a turnkey OCR system optimised for documents in historical and non-Latin scripts and by the OCR software Tesseract.

explainer.lead: PAGE is an XML standard for encoding digitised documents so that page structure and content can be described in a machine-readable way. It matters because layout analysis tools need a common encoding for both output and evaluation.

tiers.eli5: Think of a scanned page being turned into a labelled map: boxes for paragraphs, lines, words and their reading order. PAGE is one agreed way to write that map down.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers export OCR and layout-analysis results as PAGE XML so that regions, lines, words and reading order can be exchanged between tools. A pitfall is that the standard is comparable to, not identical with, ALTO, so conversion between the two needs care.
tiers.paperLevel: PAGE XML encodes page content (regions, lines, words, glyphs, reading order, text), evaluation of layout analysis (evaluation profiles and results), and cutting grids for the document image; it is maintained by PRIMA at the University of Salford. Its limits are those of an XML schema: it describes structure and text, not the image processing that produced them.

explainer.example: A scanned newspaper page is encoded with region elements for headlines and columns, line and word elements carrying text, and a reading-order list; evaluation elements can then record scores for a layout analyser on that page.
